1437	are well-motivated and can greatly improve our knowledge of PDFs at low- and high-$x$, resummed QCD, and EW couplings.

1439	Additionally, due to the cleanliness of the collider environment (in comparison to $pp$ collisions) and the increased c.m.e~reach over the LHC, 
1440	the LHeC offers a complementary opportunity to search for new physics.
1441	
1442	In particular, the LHeC is capable of probing regions of LRSM parameter space inaccessible to the 
1443	LHC~\cite{Blaksley:2011ey,Duarte:2014zea,Mondal:2015zba,Lindner:2016lxq}.
1444	
1445	The LRSM can be tested at the LHeC through searches for heavy $N$ through the process,
1446	\begin{equation}
1447	 e^- p ~\rightarrow ~N ~j ~+~ X,	\quad\text{where}\quad 		N\rightarrow \ell^{'\pm}q\overline{q'},
1448	 \label{eq:disProcess}
1449	\end{equation}
1450	which is mediated by $t$-channel $\WR$ exchange and is shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:feynmanDIS}.
1451	
1452	Initial search strategies~\cite{Mondal:2015zba,Lindner:2016lxq} have proposed requiring three high-$p_T$ jets in the central region of the detector.

1456	Eq.~(\ref{eq:disProcess}) involves the exchange of a gauge boson with a mass much larger than the collider, 
1457	and hence momentum transfer scale, i.e., $\MWR^2\gg \vert\hat{t}\vert$.
1458	This implies that the spectator jet has no natural momentum scale, unlike the decay products of $N$, which scale like $m_N$.

1491	\subsection{Kinematics of Neutrino and Top Jets at NLO+PS in LHC Collisions}\label{sec:jetKin}
1492	Heavy neutrinos and top quarks originating from $\WR$ (or $\ZR$) decays carry characteristic transverse momenta that scale as 
1493	$p_T\sim \MWR/2$. For $\MWR\gg m_{N,t}$, such neutrinos and tops are highly Lorentz boosted.
1494	Subsequently, their decays to leptons and/or quarks, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:Decay}, are highly collimated,
1495	and lead to the formation of heavy neutrino jets~\cite{Ferrari:2000sp,Mitra:2016kov} and top quark jets~\cite{Baur:2007ck,Thaler:2008ju,Kaplan:2008ie}.
1496	
1497	In this section we compare kinematics of neutrino, top, and light quark jets from high-mass $\MWR$ decays at NLO+PS accuracy.
1498	
1499	We describe our computational setup in Sec.~\ref{sec:setup}.
1500	
1501	The $N\rightarrow \ell^\pm q\overline{q'}$ branching fraction is 100\%; for $t$, we allow both hadronic and leptonic decays of the SM $W$.
1502	
1503	
1504	
1505	Events topologies are studied by first identifying charged lepton candidates, 
1506	then clustering all residual objects, including potentially misidentified leptons, into jets.
1507	
1508	Stable charged leptons $\ell\in\{e,\mu\}$ are considered hadronically isolated if 
1509	the scalar sum of transverse energy $(E_T)$ over all neighboring hadrons $X$ within a distance of $\Delta R_{\ell X}<0.3$
1510	is less than $10\%$ of the lepton's $E_T$, i.e.,
1511	\begin{equation}
1512	\sum_{X\in\{\text{hadrons}\}} E_{T}^{X} / E_{T}^{\ell} < 0.1~\quad\text{for}\quad~\Delta R_{\ell X} < 0.3.
1513	\end{equation}
1514	
1515	At the 13 TeV LHC, charged lepton candidates are then defined as hadronically isolated leptons that meet the following kinematic, 
1516	fiducial, and lepton isolation requirements~\cite{CMS:2015kjy}:
1517	\begin{equation}
1518	p_T^{\ell} > 35\GeV, ~\quad \vert \eta^\ell\vert < 2.4, ~\quad \Delta R_{\ell\ell'} > 0.3.
1519	\end{equation}
1520	
1521	We cluster all remaining constituents into jets according to the 
1522	Cambridge/Aachen (C/A) algorithm~\cite{Dokshitzer:1997in,Wobisch:1998wt} with a separation scale of $R = 1.0$.
1523	
1524	We ignore clustered jets with $p_T<20\GeV$~\cite{ATLAS:2016ecs}.
1525	
1526	Charged leptons and jets are ordered according to their $p_T$ (hardness), with $p_{T}^{j_i} > p_{T}^{j_{(i+1)}}$.
1527	
1528	To select for top quarks and heavy neutrinos, we apply the following mass cut on the hardest jet, $j_1$:
1529	\begin{equation}
1530	  \vert m_{j_1} - m_t \vert  < 25\GeV.
1531	\end{equation}
1532	The NLO+PS \-accurate cross section before and after the jet mass cut are:
1533	\begin{eqnarray}
1534	  \sigma^{\rm NLOPS}:\qquad	& 14.0~(36.7)~[76.3]\fb	&			\quad\text{for~the }~	N~(t)~[q]	\quad\text{channel},\\
1535	  \sigma^{\rm NLOPS+\text{$m_j$}~Cut}:\qquad	& 8.39~(9.69)~[9.16]\fb	&	\quad\text{for~the }~	N~(t)~[q]	\quad\text{channel}
1536	\end{eqnarray}
1537	We see that the $m_j$ (accidentally) brings the individual rates to a very comparable level, avoid the need for any additional type of normalization.
1538	Without the cut, the quark channels are much larger due to branching fractions that are $3-6\times$ larger.
1539	
1540	To reconstruct $\WR$ kinematics, we drop the jet mass cut and sum the momenta of the two hardest jets
1541	in the quark channels, or hardest jet and lepton in the neutrino channel.

1580	In Fig.~\ref{fig:effLRSMnlo_pp_wr_Xjet_pTj1}, we show the $p_T$ distribution of $j_1$.
1581	The Jacobian peak at $p_T \sim \MWR/2 \sim 1.5\TeV$ is clearly visible,
1582	but is noticeably broader for $t$ and $q$ jets than $N$ jets.
1583	
1584	With respect to LO+PS, quark jets possess a varying differential $K$-Factor that falls below $\confirm{1}$ for $p_T\lesssim1\TeV$,
1585	and grows to $K_{p_T}^{\rm NLOPS}\sim1.2$ for larger $p_T$.
1586	For neutrino jets, $K_{p_T}^{\rm NLOPS}\approx 1.2$ and is approximately constant across all $p_T$.
1587	Numerically, $K_{p_T}^{\rm NLOPS}\approx 1.2$ is very close to the total inclusive NLO $K$-factor for $\WR$ production, 
1588	which is driven by virtual and soft corrections.
1589	
1590	We attribute the differences in broadening and $K_{p_T}^{\rm NLOPS}$ simply to the fact that quarks carry net color charge, unlike neutrinos:
1591	
1592	Quark jets are susceptible to hard, wide-angle FSR that carry away momentum and causes broadening in the $p_T$ spectrum.
1593	In DY-type processes, this is more accurately modeled by matrix element corrections that first appear at NLO in QCD than by parton showers.

1596	In Fig.~\ref{fig:effLRSMnlo_pp_wr_Xjet_yj1} is the rapidity $(y)$ distribution of $j_1$.
1597	Compared to quark jets, heavy neutrino jets possesses a broader, flatter distribution.
1598	With respect to LO+PS, again, $K_{p_T}^{\rm NLOPS}\approx 1.2$ and is approximately constant for neutrino jets.
1599	For quarks jets, we observe a depletion of events with larger rapidities, and is consistent with the $p_T$ spectrum at NLO+PS.
1600

1602	
1603	We show in Fig.~\ref{fig:effLRSMnlo_pp_wr_Xjet_mj1} the jet mass distribution centered about $m_t$.
1604	For heavy neutrino and top jets, the resonant peak around $m_t$ is unambiguous.
1605	As the light quark jet contribution is a continuum at this mass scale, it is featureless.
1606	
1607	Most striking is the upward shift in the top jet mass compared to the neutrino jet mass.
1608	The shift is caused, in part, by the production of an off-shell top that then emits a (semi-)collinear radiation and is brought on-shell.
1609	The collinear nature of the emission means it is captured by the sequential jet algorithm and is well-modeled by parton showers.
1610	As $\MWR\gg m_t$, such a configuration is not phase space suppressed.
1611	Non-perturbative and large finite width effects are also important\cite{Skands:2007zg,Hoang:2008xm}.
1612	For more details, see, e.g., \cite{Skands:2007zg,Hoang:2008xm} and references therein.
1613	
1614	However, as neutrinos are not subject to such effects, $N$ jets retains their narrow, resonant structure, even after showering and hadronization.
1615	This suggests that searches for neutrino jets, as proposed by~\cite{Ferrari:2000sp,Mitra:2016kov},
1616	may be able to impose much more aggressive invariant mass cuts than the 15 GeV presently used in LHC top quark mass studies~\cite{Aad:2015waa}.

1620	In Fig.~\ref{fig:effLRSMnlo_pp_wr_Xjet_mj1Hemi1} we plot the ratio of $m_{j_1}/M_{\rm Hemisphere}$,
1621	where $M_{\rm Hemisphere}$ is the hemisphere mass associated with $j_1$.
1622	We define the hemisphere mass of the leading jet simply as the invariant mass of all jet momenta $p_k$ in the same hemisphere as $j_1$, i.e.,
1623	\begin{equation}
1624	 M_{\rm Hemisphere} = \sqrt{p_{\rm Hemisphere}^2},	\quad\text{where}\quad
1625	 p_{\rm Hemisphere} = \sum_{k\in\{jets\}} p_k 		\quad\text{and}\quad
1626	 \hat{p}_k\cdot\hat{p}_{j_1} > 1.
1627	 \label{eq:mHemiDef}
1628	\end{equation}
1629	Due to the large $\WR$ mass we consider, it is largely at rest in $\sqrt{s}=13\TeV$ collisions.
1630	This is supported by Fig.~\ref{fig:effLRSMnlo_pp_wr_Xjet_pTWRreco}.
1631	Subsequently, while not rigorously infrared-collinear safe, 
1632	the axis defined by the direction of hardest jet is the thrust axis to a good approximation, justifying the use of Eq.~(\ref{eq:mHemiDef}).
1633	
1634	The utility of this ratio is its sensitivity to radiation associated with a parton but missed by a jet algorithm because the emission angle is too wide,
1635	e.g., high-$p_T$, wide angle FSR off a top quark that falls outside the top jet's radius.
1636	
1637	Due to the presence of non-global logarithms and jet substructure, as well as parton shower dependence,
1638	a complete and systematic study of hemisphere variables is outside the narrow scope of this report.
1639	For further details, see~\cite{Dasgupta:2001sh,Banfi:2006gy,Banfi:2010pa,Fischer:2014bja} and references therein.
1640	
1641	In the context of the C/A algorithm, the ratio can be interpreted as the mass ratio of a jet with $R=1$ to that of a ``larger'' jet with $R\approx\pi/2$.
1642	
1643	In all three channels, we find a sizable fraction of events are concentrated at $0.9 < m_{j_1}/M_{\rm Hemisphere} < 1$,
1644	indicating that single the hardest jet from high-mass $\WR$ decays contains most all the radiation one one side of the detector.
1645	As expected, fewer quark jet events satisfy this property.
1646	
1647	The accumulation at smaller ratios is due to the large contamination from ISR, which is supported by the flat $N$ jet differential $K$-factor.

1682	Categorically, we observe that neutrino jets possess largely constant differential $K$-factors.
1683	This is qualitatively different from quark jets, which feature more dynamical $K_{\mathcal{O}}$.
1684	
1685	The result follows from the color-singlet nature of the $pp\rightarrow \WR^\pm \rightarrow Ne^\pm$ process
1686	and large mass (in comparison to the total beam c.m.~energy) of the intermediate $\WR$:
1687	
1688	Since $N$ and $e$ are color neutral, they do not undergo QCD FSR, implying that all QCD corrections 
1689	are confined to the $q\overline{q'}\rightarrow \WR^{*}$ subprocess.
1690	However, due to the large $\MWR$ considered, high-$p_T$ ISR is phase space-suppressed, leaving only hard-collinear (HC) and soft ISR.
1691	
1692	HC radiation is encapsulated in the definitions of PDFs and parton showers, and therefore is the same at LO and NLO.
1693	
1694	For high-mass DY processes, in both the SM and generic BSM scenarios,
1695	virtual corrections and soft radiation amplitudes factorize into the Born amplitude and universal form factors that 
1696	combine (due to the KLN theorem) into a finite QCD scaling factor.
1697	
1698	Subsequently, total and differential NLO in QCD $K$-factors for high-mass DY systems are constant, up to running of $\alpha_s(\mu)$.

1704	\section{Summary and Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
1705	The LRSM is a predictive and economic extension of the SM 
1706	that explains several observations not accommodated by the SM.
1707	
1708	It postulates the existence of the $\WR,\ZR,$ gauge bosons and Majorana neutrinos $N$, 
1709	that may be discovered/studied at the LHC or near-future collider experiment.
1710	
1711	We report the construction of a new MC model file capable of simulating fully differential benchmark 
1712	$\WR,\ZR,$ and $N$ production and decay processes at an accuracy up to NLO+PS using the FR+\mgamc+PY8 framework. 
1713	
1714	Such corrections are necessary to realistically model QCD radiation at hadron super colliders.
1715	
1716	Remarkably fewer input parameters are required in comparison to LO LRSM implementations.
1717	
1718	Publicly available UFO files~\cite{nloFRModel} are compatible with similar general-purpose event generators, e.g., 
1719	HERWIG and SHERPA.
1720	
1721	Our NLO in QCD corrections and residual scale uncertainty for inclusive $pp\rightarrow\WR,\ZR$ production at the 13 TeV LHC and 100 TeV VLHC 
1722	are in agreement with other findings.
1723	
1724	This is similarly the case for inclusive $e^-p\rightarrow N+X$ production at a future LHeC experiment.
1725	
1726	
1727	As a case study, we have investigated at NLO+PS accuracy,
1728	the kinematics of heavy neutrino jets and top jets originating from the decay of high-mass $\WR$ decays at the 13 TeV LHC.
1729	
1730	With respect to LO+PS, we find \confirm{appreciable} changes to top jet kinematics that we attribute hard, wide-angle FSR not captured by parton showers.
1731	
1732	Conversely, due to the absence of such FSR, we find neutrino jets kinematics are resilient against the effects of parton showers and hadronization.
1733	This suggests that in searches for neutrino jets, 
1734	aggressive selection cuts that would otherwise be inappropriate for top jets can be imposed with minimal signal loss.

1840	\section{User Defined Generator-Level Cuts in \mgamc}\label{app:GenCuts}
1841	Imposing phase space cuts on final-state top quarks and heavy neutrinos in~\mgamc~
1842	requires modifying the file \texttt{SubProcesses/cuts.f} in the local process directory, i.e.,
1843	the directory \texttt{PP\_WR\_Ne\_NLO} or \texttt{PP\_WR\_tb\_NLO} if following App.~\ref{app:sigDef}.

1845	we insert after Line 377 of \texttt{cuts.f} the following:

2500	NO TOOLS: this run has no file, shell, network or code tools. Everything you need is in
2501	this message: the Standard Model file SM.fr (the file this add-on is loaded on top of:
2502	take field names, index conventions and hypercharges from it) and the paper. Do not ask
2503	for anything; do the extraction and write the model.
2504	
2505	## Physics-completeness rules (apply to every model)
2506	
2507	1. Free-field terms for every new particle class. Write a named kinetic + mass term for each new field even when the paper shows only L_int. Use the mass symbol declared in the class `Mass -> {M, value}`. Add the term to the total Lagrangian sum.
2508	   - Real vector (gauge singlet): `LXkin := -1/4 FS[X, mu, nu] FS[X, mu, nu] + 1/2 MX^2 X[mu] X[mu];` (the explicit form `-1/4 (del[X[nu], mu] - del[X[mu], nu])^2` is equivalent).
2509	   - Complex vector: `-1/2 FS[Xbar, mu, nu] FS[X, mu, nu] + MX^2 Xbar[mu] X[mu]`.
2510	   - Complex scalar: `DC[phibar, mu] DC[phi, mu] - Mphi^2 phibar phi`. Real scalar: `1/2 del[phi, mu] del[phi, mu] - 1/2 Mphi^2 phi^2`.
2511	   - Dirac fermion: `I psibar.Ga[mu].DC[psi, mu] - Mpsi psibar.psi`. Majorana fermion (`SelfConjugate -> True`): `I/2 psibar.Ga[mu].del[psi, mu] - 1/2 Mpsi psibar.psi`.
2512	
2513	2. Explicit EFT cutoffs. When the paper writes an operator with `1/Lambda^n` (or `1/M^n`, `1/f^n`), declare each distinct cutoff as an External parameter in GeV with the paper's benchmark value, e.g. `Lam == { ParameterType -> External, Value -> 1000., BlockName -> CUTOFF, InteractionOrder -> {QED, -1}, Description -> "EFT cutoff [GeV], Eq.(N)" }`. Write the factor `1/Lam^(d-4)` verbatim in the term, with `d` the operator mass dimension you computed in the self-audit. Keep the paper's dimensionless couplings (kappa, lambda, c_i) dimensionless with the paper's benchmark defaults. Do this for the term and for its `HC[...]` partner. Only if the paper's own implementation absorbs `kappa/Lambda^n` into one coefficient may you do the same; then the parameter Description must say "= kappa/Lambda^n, mass dimension -n, units GeV^-n" and the default must equal the paper's numeric `kappa/Lambda^n`. 2514	
2515	3. Charge conjugation. When the paper writes a fermion with a charge-conjugation superscript (`psi^c`, `\bar{psi^c}`, `psi^T C`, or a Majorana mass eigenstate that enters a chiral current with the opposite chirality), write it as `CC[psi]` (and `bar[CC[psi]]` for the conjugated bar). Never write the bare field. If the paper's benchmark sets that term's coefficient to zero, either drop the term or write it with `CC[...]`; never keep the term with the conjugation dropped. Use the class field with its Generation index (for example the SM class `vl[ff]`), not a class member like `ve[nn]`, because FeynRules reads an index on a class member as a spin index.
2516	
2517	4. SU(2) doublet contractions. Use the SM.fr conventions the add-on loads on: `Phi` has Y = +1/2, `LL` has Y = -1/2, `QL` has Y = +1/6, `Phi[1] = -I GP`, `Phi[2] = (vev + H + I G0)/Sqrt[2]`. Contract a doublet with an anti-doublet on a shared index: `LLbar[sp, ii, ff] ... Phi[ii]`. Contract two objects of the same conjugation type (`LLbar` with `Phibar`, `QLbar` with `Phibar`, i.e. any term the paper writes with `Htilde = i tau2 H*`) with `Eps[ii, jj]` on two distinct indices: `LLbar[sp, ii, ff] ... Phibar[jj] Eps[ii, jj]`. Never contract `LLbar[ii]` with `Phibar[ii]`. Model the SM Yukawas: `QLbar.dR Phi[ii]`, `LLbar.lR Phi[ii]`, `QLbar.uR Phibar[jj] Eps[ii, jj]`.
2518	
2519	5. New U(1) charges. Do not copy a paper's charge table literally when the paper's Yukawa equation and its table use different hypercharge conventions (for example the paper effectively uses Y(H) = -1/2). Re-derive the new-U(1) charge of every SM field, including the Higgs, from the requirement that all SM Yukawas and all new Yukawas are invariant under SM.fr conventions. Report which sign you chose and why. Do not put quantum numbers on a `SelfConjugate -> True` class; put a chiral charge on an Unphysical chiral class instead.
2520	
2521	6. Read only the paper. Do not open any cached or reference `.fr` file for the same model. If you see one, say so in the output and do not use it.
2522	
2523	7. Fractions and roots in extracted equations. The paper text is machine-extracted. A displayed fraction or radical can arrive flattened: the numerator, the fraction bar and the denominator become separate lines, so `A / Sqrt[B]` and `A Sqrt[B]` look identical. For every coefficient that contains a fraction, a square root or a power:
2524	   - If a LaTeX source file (`*_source.tex`) is available, read the `\frac{...}{...}` and `\sqrt{...}` there and take it literally. The LaTeX is authoritative over the flattened text.
2525	   - Otherwise cross-check the placement against a second equation of the paper that depends on the same coefficient (a partial width, a cross section, a limit, or a small-parameter expansion) and name that equation in the self-audit. A coupling `g/Sqrt[1-x]` gives a width proportional to `1/(1-x)`; a coupling `g Sqrt[1-x]` gives a width proportional to `(1-x)`.
2526	   - If neither resolves it, choose the form that reproduces a numerical value the paper states, and say so.
2527	   Never silently pick one placement.
2528	
2529	8. Mass mixing. When the paper diagonalises a mass mixing between a new state and an SM state (Z-Z', h-S, W-W_R, nu-N), write the mass eigenstates the paper uses: declare the mixing angle (External, or Internal with the paper's formula) and express the gauge eigenstates through it in `Definitions` of Unphysical classes. Do not leave the mixing in a comment.
2530	
2531	## FeynRules and UFO construct rules (each one broke a compile or a MadGraph import in earlier runs)

2533	9. Non-fundamental colour representations. 2534	
2535	10. Names. Class names, parameter names and index names must not be Mathematica built-ins or FeynRules symbols: never `N`, `C`, `D`, `E`, `I`, `K`, `O`, `HC`, `CC`, `FS`, `DC`, `del`, `Eps`, `Ga`, `ProjP`, `ProjM`, and never a name SM.fr already declares (`H`, `Phi`, `Z`, `W`, `A`, `G`, `ee`, `gs`, `gw`, `sw`, `cw`, `vev`, `MZ`, `MW`, ...). 2539	12. Tensor parameters. Give every indexed parameter explicit per-component values (`yN[1,1] -> 0.1, yN[1,2] -> 0, ...`; schema: `value_rules`). Never use a pattern rule such as `X[i_?NumericQ, j_?NumericQ] :> ...` in `Definitions`: FeynRules exports the pattern verbatim as a UFO parameter name and MadGraph fails with an unrelated "invalid syntax" error.
2540	
2541	13. Flavour structure in matrix form. Write generation-space couplings as matrix products between class fields, `uqbar.VCKMR.Ga[mu].ProjP.dq`, `LLbar.yN.NR`, `ISbar.Ga[mu].ProjM.IS`, not as explicit index sums `VCKMR[ff1, ff2] uqbar[ff1, cc]...dq[ff2, cc]`, and never nest one generation index inside another. 2543	14. One declared total. Define exactly one Lagrangian term named `LTotal` that sums every other term you define, and make sure every other term appears in that sum. 2545	15. Declarations. Every field used in a term is declared; every parameter used in a term is declared with a numeric default; every `SelfConjugate -> True` class has no `QuantumNumbers`; a Majorana mass term is `-1/2 M psibar.psi`.
